How to use this primer

This booklet teaches solar photovoltaics from zero, in the order the exam needs it. Read it once before the Complete Solutions. Each section has a green core idea box (learn this first), the key figure, the formulas with every symbol and unit, and a short worked example. Section A (cell physics) is mostly explain with a diagram, with a few short numericals (photocurrent, Vbi, W, carrier densities, fill factor). Section B (systems) is half descriptive and half numericals that repeat (temperature derating, inverter selection, SHS (solar home system) sizing, life-cycle cost).

The pass set (from the Question Map): A1-A6 and B1-B7; A7 (thin film) and A8 (multi-junction, perovskite, generations) are the next to add.

The whole course on one page

Read the map from left to right. Physics: a semiconductor absorbs a photon and makes an electron-hole pair; a p-n junction separates the pair, giving current and voltage. Device: the cell is described by its I-V curve (Isc, Voc, FF (fill factor), η) and loses energy in known ways. Technology: silicon wafers, thin films and multi-junction cells. System: cells make modules and arrays; a controller, battery and inverter deliver the energy to loads or the grid; sizing and economics decide how big and whether it pays.

Constants, units and maths refresher

Keep these constants on your answer script; most Section A numericals use only them. Work in cm for semiconductor numbers (doping in cm−3, ε in F/cm) and in SI for light (W/m2, m).

QuantityValue
electron charge q1.602 × 10−19 C (also 1 eV = 1.602 × 10−19 J)
Planck h; speed of light c6.626 × 10−34 J·s; 2.998 × 108 m/s; hc = 1240 eV·nm
thermal voltage kT/q at 300 K0.0258 V (k = 1.381 × 10−23 J/K = 8.617 × 10−5 eV/K)
permittivity ε0; Si εr8.854 × 10−14 F/cm; 11.7
Si at 300 KEg = 1.12 eV, ni = 1.5 × 1010 cm−3 (some books 9.65 × 109), NC = 3.22 × 1019, NV = 1.83 × 1019 cm−3
STC (standard test conditions (1000 W/m2, AM1.5, 25 °C))1000 W/m2, AM1.5 spectrum, 25 °C cell
length and area1 μm = 10−4 cm = 10−6 m; 1 nm = 10−9 m; 1 cm2 = 10−4 m2; 1 mA/cm2 = 10 A/m2

Exponentials and logarithms

  • ex grows very fast: the diode current doubles for every 18 mV of extra forward voltage at 300 K. e−x decays fast: light intensity e−αx falls to 37% after one absorption length 1/α, to 2% after 4/α.
  • ln undoes e: if I/I0 = eqV/kT then V = (kT/q) ln(I/I0). ln(10) = 2.303, so Voc rises by 0.0258 × 2.303 = 59.5 mV for a tenfold increase in light.
  • Powers of ten: (1.5 × 1010)2 = 2.25 × 1020; 1016 × 1018 = 1034; divide exponents by subtracting.

Energy, power and battery units

  • Power (W) = V × I. Energy (Wh) = power × hours. 1 kWh = 1000 Wh = 3.6 MJ.
  • Battery capacity (Ah) × voltage (V) = stored energy (Wh): 200 Ah × 12 V = 2.4 kWh. Usable energy = capacity × DOD (depth of discharge).
  • Peak sun hours: daily solar energy in kWh/m2 written as hours of 1000 W/m2. 5 kWh/m2/day = 5 PSH (peak sun hours), so a 100 Wp module gives about 500 Wh/day before losses.

Semiconductors and doping (A1)

In a crystal, electron energies form a valence band (bonded electrons) and a conduction band (free electrons), separated by the bandgap Eg. Breaking a bond makes a free electron and a hole. Adding phosphorus (5 valence electrons) gives extra electrons: n-type; adding boron (3) gives extra holes: p-type. The Fermi level EF shows where electrons are: near EC in n-type, near EV in p-type.

n · p = ni2; n = NCe−(EC−EF)/kT; p = NVe−(EF−EV)/kT

SymbolMeaningUnit
n, pelectron and hole densitiescm−3
niintrinsic carrier densitycm−3
ND, NAdonor and acceptor dopingcm−3
NC, NVeffective density of states of CB and VBcm−3
EC, EV, EFconduction band edge, valence band edge, Fermi leveleV

Example: NA = 1016: p = 1016, n = 2.25 × 1020/1016 = 2.25 × 104 cm−3.

Carriers move by drift (pushed by an electric field, speed = μE) and diffusion (spreading from high to low concentration, D). They are linked: D = μkT/q.

Light in, carriers out: absorption and recombination (A2)

A photon with energy E = hc/λ ≥ Eg can be absorbed and make one electron-hole pair. Light intensity decays as e−αx. The extra carriers live for a lifetime τ and wander a diffusion length L = √(Dτ) before they recombine: radiatively (photon), via a defect (SRH, heat), by Auger (energy to a third carrier) or at the surface.

Eph (eV) = 1240/λ (nm); Φ0 = Pλ/(hc); Φ(x) = (1 − R)Φ0e−αx; Jph = q × (absorbed photon flux)

SymbolMeaningUnit
λwavelengthnm or m
Pirradiance (light power per area)W/m2
Φphoton fluxm−2s−1
Rfront reflectancefraction
αabsorption coefficientcm−1 or m−1
Jphphotocurrent densityA/m2

Example: 500 nm photon: 1240/500 = 2.48 eV (more than Si’s 1.12 eV, so absorbed; the extra 1.36 eV becomes heat). 1000 W/m2 of it is 2.52 × 1021 photons/m2s; with 38% reflected, J = 1.602 × 10−19 × 0.62 × 2.52 × 1021 = 250 A/m2.

The p-n junction and the solar cell (A3)

Join p and n material: carriers diffuse across and leave behind fixed ions, forming a depletion region with a built-in electric field and voltage Vbi. Light-made electrons and holes that reach this field are separated: electrons go to n, holes to p. That separation is the photocurrent and the photovoltage.

Vbi = (kT/q) ln(NAND/ni2); W = √[(2ε/q)(Vbi − V)(1/NA + 1/ND)]; Emax ≈ 2Vbi/W

SymbolMeaningUnit
Vbibuilt-in voltageV
Wdepletion widthcm
εεrε0 = 1.036 × 10−12 for SiF/cm
Vapplied voltage (negative for reverse bias)V
Emaxpeak electric fieldV/cm

Example: NA = 1016, ND = 1018: Vbi = 0.0258 ln(1034/2.25 × 1020) = 0.81 V; W = 0.325 μm; Emax = 5 × 104 V/cm.

In a p-i-n cell an undoped layer sits between p and n; the field fills it, so carriers are collected by drift (needed for amorphous Si and perovskites, whose diffusion lengths are short).

The I-V curve and the equivalent circuit (A4)

A solar cell is a current source (light) in parallel with a diode (the junction). Short-circuit gives Isc; open circuit gives Voc; in between there is one point of maximum power. The fill factor says how square the curve is. Real cells add a series resistance (lowers FF near Voc) and a shunt resistance (lowers FF near Isc).

I = IL − I0[eq(V+IRs)/nkT − 1] − (V + IRs)/Rsh; Voc = (kT/q) ln(IL/I0 + 1); FF = VmIm/(VocIsc); η = VocIscFF/(GA)

SymbolMeaningUnit
ILlight-generated current (≈ Isc)A
I0dark saturation currentA
nideality factor (1-2)–
Rs, Rshseries and shunt resistanceΩ
Vm, Imvoltage and current at the maximum power pointV, A
GirradianceW/m2
Acell or module aream2

Example: Voc = 0.6 V, Isc = 3.5 A, Vm = 0.5 V, Im = 3.1 A, 100 cm2: Pm = 1.55 W; FF = 1.55/2.1 = 0.738; η = 1.55/(1000 × 0.01) = 15.5%.

Losses and limits (A5)

Photons below Eg pass through (non-absorption); photons above Eg waste their extra energy as heat (thermalisation). These two set the Shockley-Queisser limit: about 33.7% at Eg = 1.34 eV for one junction. Practical losses add on top: reflection, shading by fingers, recombination, resistance.

The cures map one-to-one: texture + ARC (reflection), thin fingers (shading), passivation + BSF (recombination), heavy doping under contacts (resistance), multi-junction (both spectral losses).

Making silicon cells (A6)

Sand/quartz → arc furnace (MG-Si, 98%) → trichlorosilane → distillation → Siemens reactor (polysilicon, 9N) → Czochralski ingot → wire-sawn wafers → texture, phosphorus diffusion, SiNx ARC (anti-reflection coating), screen-printed contacts, firing → tested cell.

Thin films and advanced cells (A7, A8)

Direct-gap materials (CdTe, CIGS (copper indium gallium diselenide), GaAs, perovskite) absorb sunlight in 1-3 μm, so cells can be thin films on glass. Multi-junction cells stack several gaps (largest on top) so each photon is used by a junction just below its energy; they must be matched in bandgap, current and lattice constant.

From cell to array; light and heat (B1)

Series: voltages add, current stays. Parallel: currents add, voltage stays. Current is proportional to light and area; voltage falls as the cell heats up (about −2.3 mV/°C per Si cell), so power falls about 0.45% per °C above 25 °C.

P(T) = PSTC[1 + γ(T − 25)]; Isc(G) = Isc,STC × G/1000; Ns = Vneeded/Vm,cell; Np = Ineeded/Im

SymbolMeaningUnit
γtemperature coefficient of power (−0.0045 /°C)1/°C
Tcell temperature°C
Ns, Npnumber in series and in parallel–

Example: 75 Wp at 45 °C: 75 × (1 − 0.0045 × 20) = 68.25 W.

Shading and diodes (B2)

In a series string, the shaded cell sets the current for everyone, and it can be forced into reverse bias and become a hot spot. A bypass diode (in parallel, opposite polarity) gives the current a way around; a blocking diode (in series) stops the battery discharging into the panel at night.

Battery, charge controller, MPPT (maximum power point tracking (tracker)) and converters (B3)

The charge controller keeps the battery between a high limit (stop charging) and a low limit (cut the load). A PWM (pulse width modulation) controller pulses the current near full charge. An MPPT controller is a DC-DC converter that keeps the panel at its maximum power point by matching impedance.

Buck: Vout = DVin; Boost: Vout = Vin/(1 − D); at MPP (maximum power point) dP/dV = 0 ⇔ dI/dV = −I/V; C-rate current = Ah/h

SymbolMeaningUnit
Dduty cycle = on-time/period–
Ahbattery capacityA·h
DODdepth of discharge: fraction of capacity used–

Inverters (B4)

An inverter turns DC into AC with a bridge of switches. Square wave is cheap but distorted; modified sine is in between; pure sine (PWM + filter) is clean and required for the grid. THD (total harmonic distortion) measures the distortion.

Pout = ηPin; loss = Pin − Pout; IDC = Pin/Vbattery; rating ≈ 1.25 × load; THD = √(ΣVh2)/V1

Example: 300 W in at 88%: 264 W out, 36 W lost.

System types and net metering (B5)

Off-grid: PV, controller, battery, inverter, loads. On-grid: PV, grid-tied inverter, net meter, grid (the grid is the battery). Hybrid: add a battery or a diesel/wind generator. Net metering: the meter runs both ways and you pay only for import minus export.

Sizing a solar home system (B6)

Size in this order: daily energy of the loads → PV watts → battery Ah → controller amps → inverter VA → switches → cables. Always add the 25% safety margin for the electronics and protection.

E = ΣP·n·h; PPV = E/(η·PSH); Cbat = E·days/(V·DOD); Icc = 1.25 PPV/V; Sinv = 1.25 Pload; A = 2ρLI/ΔV

SymbolMeaningUnit
Edaily load energyWh/day
PSHpeak sun hoursh/day
ηbattery charging (system) efficiency–
Cbatbattery capacityAh
ρcopper resistivity 0.0175Ω·mm2/m
Lone-way cable lengthm
ΔVallowed voltage drop (2-3% of system V)V
Aconductor cross-sectionmm2

Example: 1 kWh/day, 5 PSH, 80%: PPV = 1000/(0.8 × 5) = 250 Wp; battery for 2 days at 12 V, 50% DOD: 1000 × 2/(12 × 0.5) = 333 Ah.

Economics and ecology (B7)

Money spent in future years is worth less today. Convert every future cost to present worth, add them up (life-cycle cost), and compare systems. LCOE (levelized cost of electricity) is that cost per kWh. Energy payback time is how long the panel takes to make back the energy used to produce it (1-3 years).

x = (1 + i)/(1 + d); Pr = xn; Pa = (1 − xn)/(1 − x); ALCC (annualised life-cycle cost) = LCC (life-cycle cost)/Pa; EPBT (energy payback time) = Einvested/Eper year

SymbolMeaningUnit
iinflation ratefraction/yr
ddiscount ratefraction/yr
nyear of the cost, or lifetimeyr
Prpresent-worth factor of a one-time cost in year n–
Papresent-worth factor of a yearly cost for n years–

Example: i = 3%, d = 10%: x = 0.9364; a battery costing $900 in year 5 is worth 900 × 0.93645 = $648 today.
